description: We are a small team of young developers, all of whom desire to create an interactive map that helps astronauts explore, navigate, and simulate missions on Mars using real NASA data. Unfortunately, we're not scientists, but we can happily say that we're curious, a little chaotic, and, last but not least, utterly motivated to deliver something cool in 48 hours fueled by caffeine, bad jokes, and a completely functional prototype that actually works on our planet. By planet, of course, we mean Mars.
summary: T.A.R.S. is a web-based mission planner that lets anyone plan, budget and rehearse a crewed walk or rover drive across Jezero crater, where Perseverance landed. It turns the Martian Map challenge into a practical survival tool. It doesn’t stop at showing the terrain: it tells you whether a trip can be done safely. The map is built from real NASA and USGS orbital data: Viking, THEMIS and CTX imagery, plus MOLA, HRSC and Mars 2020 elevation models down to 1 m resolution. On this terrain, T.A.R.S. finds routes in three styles (safest, fastest and most energy-efficient) and never crosses ground steeper than the vehicle can climb. A trip budget then runs the clock along the route. It tracks time, oxygen, power, water and radiation dose, keeps a 20% oxygen reserve and marks the point of no return. Users can also check dust, temperature, daylight, live space weather and geology layers, run mission simulations, compare plans against Perseverance’s real drives, and walk the route in a first-person helmet view. This matters because the first humans on Mars will depend on safety margins. T.A.R.S. makes those margins visible, and it makes Mars exploration easy to understand for students and the public.
details:
T.A.R.S. (The Astronaut’s Routing System) is a planning and rehearsal tool for crewed excursions on Mars, centred on Jezero crater. A user picks a start and a destination, chooses to walk or drive a rover, and T.A.R.S. plans the trip and checks it before anyone leaves the base.

  • Terrain: The map is built from real orbital data. Imagery comes from Viking, THEMIS and CTX. Elevation comes from MOLA, the HRSC–MOLA blend and the Mars 2020 team’s own models of Jezero at 20 m and 1 m.
  • Routes: A route search runs on this height grid and never crosses ground steeper than the vehicle can climb. It returns three options: Safest (avoids steep, rough, cold and high-radiation ground), Fastest, and Eco (least body energy on foot, or least battery on wheels).
  • Trip budget: The planner then follows each route with the clock running. It tracks time, oxygen, power, water and radiation dose. Walking speed follows Tobler’s hiking rule, capped for a pressure suit. Metabolic cost uses the Pandolf load-carriage equation, scaled to Mars gravity. A plan passes only if nothing runs out and 20% of the oxygen is held in reserve. T.A.R.S. also marks the point of no return.
  • Walk-home rings: These show how far a crew can get on foot in 1, 2 and 4 hours over real ground. For a rover, the ring marks the furthest point from which the crew could still walk home on suit air if the rover failed, the same rule Apollo crews drove by.
  • Mission mode: The plan plays back in simulated time. The crew receives graded alerts (note, advisory, caution, warning) for steep ground, sunset, low reserves, dust devils and particle events. A rule-based base station replies using the crew’s own numbers.
  • Environment and immersion: A Mars clock uses NASA’s Mars24 method. Dust, temperature and radiation are modelled, and radiation is anchored to Curiosity RAD measurements. Live space-weather alerts come from NASA’s DONKI database. Users can also view USGS geology and CRISM mineral overlays, and walk the route in a first-person Rover/helmet view.

Benefits

  • Turns raw orbital data into a clear answer: can this trip be done safely, and with what margin?
  • Makes life-support limits visible on the map instead of hiding them in spreadsheets.
  • Is honest about what it knows. Every value is labelled as either measured (NASA/USGS data) or modelled, and each model states its limits.
  • Checks itself against reality. The planner routes five stretches of Perseverance’s actual drive and reports how closely its line matches the rover’s path.

Intended impact
T.A.R.S. helps mission designers, students and the public understand what a human walk on Mars would really demand: how far is safe, when to turn back, and how dust, darkness or a solar storm change the plan. It makes NASA’s open Mars datasets usable and engaging for people who are not planetary scientists.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, built with Vite. MapLibre GL JS renders the map and 3D terrain.
  • Performance: Web Workers handle terrain tiles, route search and walking-range calculations, so the interface stays responsive.
  • Backend: Convex syncs plans. The app is deployed on Vercel.
  • Data: NASA Mars Trek, USGS Astrogeology / PDS services, NASA DONKI, MOLA, HRSC, CTX, THEMIS, Viking, CRISM, the Mars 2020 terrain models and the USGS global geologic map.
  • AI and media: The app was developed with Claude Opus 5.5 as an AI coding assistant. The project video was produced with HeyGen HyperFrames.

How it is creative
T.A.R.S. does more than display a map: it treats the map as a survival instrument. It combines route planning, a physiological oxygen budget, the Apollo walk-back rule and live space weather in one view. Users can then “stand” on the route in a helmet view at true scale. What-if controls let them test a plan against a regional or global dust storm or a solar particle event before committing.

Factors we considered

  • Safety margins: a fixed oxygen reserve, the point of no return and the walk-home limit.
  • Scientific honesty: a clear line between measured and modelled data. Relief exaggeration is always shown. Simulated hazards are labelled as illustrative, not forecasts.
  • Data limits: the grid cannot see hazards smaller than one cell, HiRISE coverage is partial, and the human figures are scaled from Earth and Apollo data.
  • Usability and accessibility: a light-panel mode, spoken mission alerts and shareable view links.
  • Performance: heavy terrain and routing computations run in background workers.
